clinicalPearls: Classic triad is episodic flushing, secretory diarrhea, and bronchospasm/wheezing, but full triad is present in only a minority of patients
Syndrome typically only manifests once hepatic metastases are present, since liver normally clears vasoactive mediators from portal circulation before they reach systemic circulation
Midgut (small bowel/appendiceal) tumors are the classic cause; bronchial and other extra-intestinal primaries can bypass hepatic first-pass metabolism and cause symptoms without liver metastases
Right-sided (and occasionally left-sided) valvular heart disease from fibrotic plaque deposition is a hallmark late complication and a major driver of morbidity/mortality
Flushing is usually dry, reddish-violet, and involves face/neck/upper trunk, lasting minutes; triggers include alcohol, certain foods, emotional stress, and palpation of the tumor
Niacin deficiency (pellagra-like features) can occur because tryptophan is diverted toward serotonin synthesis rather than niacin production
Carcinoid crisis — profound flushing, bronchospasm, and hemodynamic instability — can be precipitated by anesthesia, tumor manipulation, or invasive procedures and requires pre-procedural prophylaxis
harrison.pathophysiology: Carcinoid syndrome arises from a neuroendocrine tumor (most often midgut origin) that secretes serotonin and other vasoactive substances (histamine, tachykinins, prostaglandins, kallikrein) directly into the systemic circulation, bypassing hepatic inactivation once liver metastases develop or when the primary tumor drains outside the portal system. These circulating mediators produce the characteristic flushing, diarrhea, and bronchoconstriction, while chronic exposure to serotonin and related factors promotes fibrous plaque deposition on cardiac valves, producing carcinoid heart disease.
additionalDifferentials: Systemic mastocytosis / mast cell activation syndrome
VIPoma or other functional pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors
Medullary thyroid carcinoma with calcitonin/other peptide secretion
nonInfectiousMimics: Irritable bowel syndrome (for the diarrhea component)
Alcohol-induced flushing (especially in those with aldehyde dehydrogenase variants)
additionalInvestigations: 24-hour urinary 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid (5-HIAA) — main biochemical marker of serotonin turnover, though affected by diet and certain drugs
Plasma chromogranin A — general neuroendocrine tumor marker, useful for diagnosis and monitoring tumor burden
Serum serotonin level — supportive but less specific/standardized than urinary 5-HIAA
Somatostatin receptor imaging (e.g., 68Ga-DOTATATE PET/CT) — localizes primary tumor and metastases with high sensitivity
Cross-sectional imaging (contrast CT or MRI abdomen) — assesses primary tumor site, liver metastases, and mesenteric fibrosis
Echocardiography — screens for carcinoid heart disease (tricuspid/pulmonic valve involvement)
Endoscopy/enteroscopy or capsule endoscopy — identifies small bowel primary when suspected
redFlags: Signs of carcinoid heart disease (new murmur, right heart failure symptoms) warrant urgent echocardiography and cardiology referral
Pre-procedural or pre-anesthetic patients with known/suspected carcinoid require prophylaxis to prevent carcinoid crisis
Acute severe flushing with hypotension or bronchospasm suggests evolving carcinoid crisis and needs emergent management
Bowel obstruction or ischemia from mesenteric fibrosis/desmoplastic reaction is a surgical emergency
Refractory diarrhea causing dehydration or electrolyte derangement needs prompt correction
pitfalls: Attributing episodic flushing/diarrhea to anxiety, menopause, or irritable bowel syndrome, delaying diagnosis for years
Obtaining urinary 5-HIAA without dietary restriction (serotonin-rich foods) or accounting for interfering medications, leading to false results
Overlooking carcinoid heart disease until advanced right heart failure develops
Failing to anticipate and prevent carcinoid crisis before surgery, biopsy, or anesthesia in a patient with known tumor
harrison.prognosis: Prognosis depends primarily on tumor grade, extent of metastatic disease, and presence of carcinoid heart disease; with modern somatostatin analog therapy and multidisciplinary management, many patients experience prolonged survival and symptom control, though cardiac involvement significantly worsens outcomes if untreated.
references: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 22e — Neuroendocrine Tumors and Carcinoid Syndrome
management: Somatostatin analogues such as octreotide or lanreotide as the mainstay to suppress secretion of serotonin and other vasoactive mediators and control flushing and diarrhoea.

Tumour-directed treatment including surgical resection or debulking, liver-directed embolisation for hepatic metastases, and peptide receptor radionuclide therapy or interferon for progressive disease.
Telotristat, a tryptophan hydroxylase inhibitor, for diarrhoea refractory to somatostatin analogues.
Prevention of carcinoid crisis with peri-procedural somatostatin analogue cover before surgery, anaesthesia or embolisation.
Niacin supplementation to prevent or treat pellagra from tryptophan diversion, and avoidance of flushing triggers such as alcohol.
Echocardiographic surveillance for carcinoid heart disease, with valve replacement for significant right-sided valvular involvement.
Multidisciplinary neuroendocrine tumour team care, with escalation for carcinoid crisis or cardiac decompensation.
